items.title: The Pushed Car
items.question: A man pushes his car up to a hotel door and immediately declares bankruptcy. What is happening?
choices: He crashed into the hotel entrance
His car loan was just denied
He ran out of fuel at the door
items.correctExplanation: He is playing Monopoly — the car token landing on a hotel means bankruptcy. The scene reads as real life until the game frame clicks.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is he is playing Monopoly. The car is a token, the hotel sits on Boardwalk, and bankruptcy is the game's verdict. Real-world readings (crashes, loans, fuel) all ignore the word 'pushes,' which is exactly how tokens move.
items.lessonContent:
Verbs betray the frame: tokens get pushed, cars get driven.
Game frames hide inside realistic scenery.
'Bankruptcy' plus 'hotel' is Monopoly vocabulary.
Reframe the nouns before solving the scene.
Share this: narrate one board game as real news.

items.title: The Surgeon's Son
items.question: A father and son are in a crash; the father dies, the boy needs surgery. The surgeon says, 'I cannot operate — he is my son.' How is this possible?
choices: The surgeon is the boy's mother
The surgeon is the boy's grandfather
items.correctAnswer: The surgeon is the boy's mother
items.correctExplanation: The surgeon is his mother. The puzzle works because 'surgeon' primes male-association, making the mother invisible to many solvers.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is the surgeon is the boy's mother. The riddle exploits the default assumption that surgeons are men; the grandfather and priest options extend the same bias. Two fathers is possible but not the classic answer.
items.lessonContent:
Stereotypes hide the simplest answers in plain sight.
Gendered role assumptions are the engine of this classic.
When a puzzle feels impossible, check your defaults.
The 'impossible' relation is usually just unassumed.
Share this: pose it to someone and time their pause.

items.title: The Late Pass
items.question: During a race you overtake the next-to-last runner. What position are you now in?
items.correctExplanation: Second to last — you take the passed runner's spot, and they drop to last. Passing near the back works exactly like passing near the front.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is second to last. You swapped with the runner you passed, so you stand where they stood. 'Last place' would require passing the final runner, and 'first place' confuses overtaking with leading.
items.lessonContent:
Overtaking swaps positions at any point in the line.
Back-of-pack passes follow identical logic to front ones.
'Pass X' always means standing where X stood.
Symmetry between race ends defeats the intuition gap.
Share this: ask someone about a late-race pass tonight.

items.title: The Electric Train
items.question: An electric train heads north at 80 km/h; the wind blows south at 20 km/h. Which way does the smoke blow?
items.correctExplanation: Electric trains produce no smoke. The speed and wind details are irrelevant noise designed to trigger a physics calculation on a non-existent phenomenon.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is there is no smoke. Electric locomotives have no combustion, so no smoke exists to blow. The wind and speed are decorative numbers meant to lure you into a vector calculation.
items.lessonContent:
Check whether the phenomenon exists before calculating its behavior.
Decorative numbers lure solvers into irrelevant math.
'Electric' is the kill word — it cancels the premise.
Read for contradictions, not just variables.
Share this: verify one phenomenon exists before calculating.

items.title: The Birthday Twice
items.question: A girl was 10 on her last birthday and will be 12 on her next birthday. How is this possible?
choices: She skipped a year in school
She is lying about her age
items.correctExplanation: She was born on February 29, so parties come every four years while age advances yearly. 'Birthday' here counts parties, not years.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is she was born on February 29. A leap-day baby's party count lags her age count, since February 29 returns quadrennially. The puzzle trades on two meanings of 'birthday': annual party versus birth-date anniversary.
items.lessonContent:
Words with multiple meanings are lateral levers.
'Birthday' can mean annual party or birth-date anniversary.
Leap-day edge cases turn calendar logic sideways.
Count what is actually being counted.
Share this: ask a leap-day baby how old they feel.

items.title: The Dark Room
items.question: You have one match and enter a cold room with a kerosene lamp, a wood stove, and a candle. What do you light first?
items.correctExplanation: The match — you must light the match before you can light anything else. The three appliances compete for attention; the prerequisite hides in plain sight.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is the match. You cannot light the lamp, stove, or candle without a flame source. The list of three objects is a distractor menu; the true first step is the tool in your hand.
items.lessonContent:
Prerequisites hide inside distractor lists.
Before choosing among options, check what enables them.
The tool in hand often precedes the menu.
Sequence questions: what must happen first?
Share this: strike one match before choosing tools.

items.title: The Two Coins
items.question: Two coins total 30 cents, and one is not a nickel. What are the two coins?
items.correctExplanation: A quarter (25¢) and a nickel (5¢). 'One is not a nickel' refers to the quarter — the other one *is* a nickel. The phrasing excludes exactly one coin from being a nickel.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is quarter and nickel. The statement 'one is not a nickel' is true of the quarter; it does not say 'neither is a nickel.' Scope ambiguity ('one' vs 'both') is the trap.
items.lessonContent:
'One is not X' does not mean 'neither is X'.
Scope quantifiers ('one', 'both', 'neither') are literal.
Check which object the quantifier actually covers.
Precise reading beats pattern guessing.
Share this: parse one tricky sentence aloud today.

items.title: The Months' Code
items.question: What occurs once in a minute, twice in a moment, but never in a thousand years?
items.correctExplanation: The letter M — minute has one M, moment has two Ms, thousand years has zero. Pure orthography, not time.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is the letter M. Count the Ms: mInute (1), moment (2), thousand years (0). The riddle masquerades as a temporal puzzle but is a spelling census.
items.lessonContent:
Temporal puzzles often resolve to orthography.
Count letters when time language appears.
'Never in X years' often means zero count in that word.
Shift frames from meaning to spelling.
Share this: count the Ms in your full name.

items.title: The Plane Crash
items.question: A plane crashes on the exact border of the US and Canada. Where do they bury the survivors?
items.correctExplanation: You don't bury survivors — they are alive. The border detail is theater; the verb 'bury' applies only to the dead.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is you do not bury survivors. Survivors, by definition, are living. The border geography is irrelevant theater designed to trigger a jurisdictional debate over a non-existent problem.
items.lessonContent:
Definitions dissolve fake dilemmas.
'Bury' implies dead; 'survivor' implies alive.
Geographic details often mask category errors.
Check the verb against the subject's state.
Share this: catch one fake dilemma this week.

items.title: The Bearded Barber
items.question: A man shaves every single day, yet he always keeps a full beard. How is this possible?
choices: He shaves other people for a living
He only shaves one cheek daily
items.correctAnswer: He shaves other people for a living
items.correctExplanation: He shaves other people for a living — a barber. The verb's object was never stated; solvers supply their own chin.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is he shaves other people for a living. 'Shaves' needs an object the sentence never gives, so readers donate their own face. Occupation splits the actor from the acted-upon.
items.lessonContent:
Transitive verbs need objects the text may withhold.
Readers donate their own face to bare verbs.
Occupation splits actors from the acted-upon.
Ask 'shaves whom?' before answering.
Share this: pose the bearded barber to a friend.

items.title: The Wetter Dryer
items.question: A bath towel soaks up water while making you dry. What common object gets wetter through the very act of drying?
items.correctExplanation: A towel — it absorbs water in the act of drying things. The subject and object of 'dries' are different: it dries you, wetting itself.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is a towel. 'Dries' is transitive here: the towel dries you while getting wetter itself. Sponges are close but the classic answer is the towel; deserts and rainbows play no drying role.
items.lessonContent:
Transitive verbs split subject from object.
'It dries' begs the question: dries what?
Absorbers get wetter through their own work.
Find both parties of every action verb.
Share this: ask what gets wetter as it dries.

items.title: The Rooftop Egg
items.question: A rooster lays an egg on a slanted roof. Which side does it roll down?
items.correctExplanation: Roosters don't lay eggs — only hens do. The slanted roof and rolling physics are a complete distractor built on a false premise.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is roosters do not lay eggs. Male chickens cannot lay eggs; the scenario is impossible before the roof angle matters. Impossible premises make all derived questions moot.
items.lessonContent:
Impossible premises nullify all follow-up logic.
Check the subject's capabilities before the scenario.
Biological facts are hard constraints on riddles.
Decorative physics cannot rescue a broken premise.
Share this: check one subject's abilities before its scenario.

items.title: The Hole Dirt
items.question: How much dirt is in a hole 3 feet deep, 6 feet long, and 4 feet wide?
items.correctExplanation: None — a hole, by definition, is the absence of dirt. The dimensions describe the void, not its contents.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is none. A hole is empty space where dirt used to be. Calculating volume answers 'how much dirt was removed,' not 'how much is in it.'
items.lessonContent:
Definitions decide contents: a hole contains absence.
'How much in' vs 'how much removed' are different questions.
Voids hold nothing by definition.
Dimensions of absence are still dimensions of absence.
Share this: describe one void by its dimensions.

items.title: The Pill Schedule
items.question: A doctor gives you three pills and says to take one every half hour. How long will the pills last?
items.correctExplanation: 60 minutes — take the first at 0:00, the second at 0:30, the third at 1:00. The interval is between doses, not after the last one.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 60 minutes. Three doses create two half-hour intervals (0→30, 30→60), not three. Fencepost error: N items make N−1 gaps.
items.lessonContent:
N events create N−1 intervals between them.
Fencepost errors hide in scheduling language.
'Take every X' measures gaps, not total doses.
Count the gaps, not the pills.
Share this: count gaps instead of posts once today.

items.title: The Stamp Dozen
items.question: How many 2-cent stamps are in a dozen?
items.correctExplanation: 12 — a dozen is 12, regardless of the stamp's denomination. The price is irrelevant to the count.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 12. A dozen means twelve. The '2-cent' detail is a distractor trying to redirect you to division or value calculation.
items.lessonContent:
A dozen is always twelve — denomination doesn't change count.
Irrelevant attributes (price, color, size) don't alter quantities.
Strip the adjective; the noun carries the number.
Dozen is a count, never a value.
Share this: price a dozen of something silly.

items.title: The Named Fragility
items.question: Name it and you destroy it: what fragile state ends the moment you speak its name?
items.correctExplanation: Silence — speaking ends it. The answer is the phenomenon itself, not an object that can be broken.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is silence. Saying the word produces sound, which ends silence. Glass breaks when dropped and promises break when betrayed — only silence breaks by being named.
items.lessonContent:
Self-referential acts can invert states.
Naming a state can instantiate its opposite.
Fragility here is logical, not material.
Check whether the verb enacts the noun.
Share this: hold a ten-second quiet contest with a friend.

items.title: The River Crossing
items.question: A man must cross a river with a fox, a chicken, and a sack of grain. The boat holds him plus one item. The fox eats the chicken if left alone; the chicken eats the grain if left alone. What is the minimum number of crossings?
items.correctExplanation: 7 crossings. The sequence requires shuttling the chicken back and forth as the 'safe' item: (1) chicken over, (2) return, (3) fox over, (4) chicken back, (5) grain over, (6) return, (7) chicken over. The chicken is the only item that can be left with either other.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 7. The chicken is the shuttle: it must be ferried back to separate the other pairs. Three items with two conflict pairs need 2N+1 = 7 trips. Fewer crossings leave a fatal pairing alone.
items.lessonContent:
Identify the 'safe' item that tolerates both others.
Shuttle the safe item to break conflict pairs.
N conflicting pairs with one safe item needs 2N+1 crossings.
Draw the state graph before counting trips.
Share this: ferry one conflict apart this week.

items.title: The Calendar Puzzle
items.question: Some months have 30 days, some have 31. How many have 28?
choices: None — February has 29 in leap years
items.correctExplanation: All twelve months reach day 28 — February stops near there while the rest continue past it. The question asks 'at least 28,' not 'exactly 28.'
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is twelve — all of them. Every month reaches day 28. The trap is hearing '28 days' and thinking 'February only,' but 30- and 31-day months also contain days 1 through 28.
items.lessonContent:
'How many have X' means 'at least X' unless 'exactly X' is stated.
Threshold questions include all who clear the bar.
February is the minimum, not the only one.
Threshold thinking beats equality thinking.
Share this: ask how many months have 28 days.

items.title: The Penguin Flight
items.question: Penguins are birds. Birds fly. Therefore penguins fly. What is wrong with this argument?
choices: The premise 'birds fly' is false as a universal
The conclusion is true for most birds
Logic does not apply to animals
items.correctAnswer: The premise 'birds fly' is false as a universal
items.correctExplanation: The premise 'birds fly' is a generalization with exceptions (penguins, ostriches, kiwis). Universal premises require zero counterexamples; one breaks the chain.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is the premise 'birds fly' is false as a universal. Logic is valid (if all birds fly, and penguins are birds, then penguins fly), but soundness fails because the first premise is not universally true. Validity ≠ soundness.
items.lessonContent:
Validity needs true premises; soundness needs both.
Generalisations with exceptions are not universal premises.
One counterexample breaks 'all'.
Check premises before trusting the chain.
Share this: test one universal claim for exceptions.

items.title: The Headless Body
items.question: Heads on one face, tails on the other, and no torso anywhere. What pocket object fits this anatomy?
items.correctExplanation: A coin — heads and tails with no body between. Body-part words name coin faces, not anatomy.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is a coin. Heads and tails are the two faces; 'body' has no referent at all. Snakes, hammers, and rivers each own real bodies or flows — only the coin fits all three clues.
items.lessonContent:
Body-part words often name faces, not anatomy.
Heads and tails are a small disc's entire vocabulary.
'No body' eliminates every living candidate.
Match all three clues before committing.
Share this: ask what has a head and tail tonight.

items.title: The Family Photo
items.question: A man looks at a photo and says, 'Brothers and sisters I have none, but this man's father is my father's son.' Who is in the photo?
items.correctExplanation: His son. 'My father's son' with no brothers = me. So 'this man's father is me' → the man in the photo is my son.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is his son: with no brothers, 'my father's son' means me, so the photo-man's father is me. Substitute inward and the chain resolves.
items.lessonContent:
Substitute known equals step by step.
'No brothers' collapses 'my father's son' to 'me'.
Chain relations by replacing each link.
Work inside-out on nested kinship phrases.
Share this: solve one kinship chain inside-out.

items.title: The Lift Button
items.question: A man lives on the 10th floor. Every morning he takes the elevator to the ground floor. Returning, if it's raining or others are in the lift, he goes to 10; otherwise he goes to 7 and walks up three flights. Why?
choices: He likes exercise on clear days
He is too short to reach the 10 button
The 10 button is broken on sunny days
items.correctAnswer: He is too short to reach the 10 button
items.correctExplanation: He's too short to reach the 10 button. Rain brings an umbrella (extends reach) or other passengers (press for him). On clear solo days, 7 is the highest he can reach.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is he is too short to reach the 10 button. The umbrella or other riders solve the reach problem; alone on dry days, he maxes at 7. The behavior is a practical workaround, not a preference or phobia.
items.lessonContent:
Physical constraints explain behavioral patterns.
Tools (umbrella) and social help (others) extend reach.
'Always' vs 'sometimes' reveals the condition.
Work backward from the exception to the constraint.
Share this: work backward from one odd habit.

items.title: The Weighty Feathers
items.question: Which is heavier: a kilogram of lead or a kilogram of feathers?
choices: They are equal — both are one kilogram
items.correctAnswer: They are equal — both are one kilogram
items.correctExplanation: Equal — a kilogram is a kilogram. Density differs, volume differs, mass is identical by definition.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — they are equal. The question fixes the mass (1 kg) for both; density and volume vary, but weight (mass × gravity) is the same. The intuition 'lead feels heavier' confuses density with mass.
items.lessonContent:
Equal mass means equal weight — density is a different property.
Definitions fix the compared quantity; intuition switches it.
'Heavier' in daily speech often means denser.
Lock the variable before comparing.
Share this: weigh one intuition against its definition.

items.title: The Sibling Count
items.question: A girl has as many brothers as sisters. Each brother has twice as many sisters as brothers. How many brothers and sisters are in the family?
items.correctExplanation: 4 sisters, 3 brothers: the girl sees 3-and-3 excluding herself, while each boy sees 4 sisters and 2 brothers. Two viewpoints, two equations, one family.
items.incorrectExplanation: Actually, the answer is 3 brothers, 4 sisters. Girl sees 3 brothers, 3 sisters (excluding herself) → equal. Boy sees 4 sisters, 2 brothers (excluding himself) → sisters are twice brothers. The two perspectives give two equations.
items.lessonContent:
Perspective shifts the counts (exclude self each time).
Write equations from each role's viewpoint.
Sisters = brothers from girl → S−1 = B.
Sisters = 2×brothers from boy → S = 2(B−1).
Share this: solve one family puzzle per viewpoint.

items.title: The Clock Strike
items.question: A clock strikes 6 times in 5 seconds. How long does it take to strike 12 at the same rate?
items.correctExplanation: 11 seconds: six strikes make 5 one-second gaps, so twelve strikes make 11 gaps. Count intervals, not strikes.
items.incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 11 seconds. Strikes are points; seconds live in the gaps between them. Six strikes give 5 gaps of one second, so twelve give 11.
items.lessonContent:
N events create N−1 intervals — the fencepost rule.
Strikes are points; time lives in the gaps.
Rate = interval duration, not event duration.
Count gaps, not ticks.
